name: Montenegro
summary_text: Montenegro decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1977, in the same year as Croatia and Slovenia, and the prohibition has not returned. The current framework comprises an anti-discrimination law that expressly covers gender identity, hate-crime provisions that list sexual orientation and gender identity as motives, and a same-sex partnership law adopted in 2020 after parliament rejected an earlier version on 31 July 2019. A visitor has no legal exposure for being trans or for presenting gender non-conformingly in public.  Two gaps shape what that framework delivers. There is no legal gender recognition statute, so change of gender markers is handled through inconsistent administrative practice rather than a defined procedure. The European Commission has also found that prosecutors overuse misdemeanour charges in place of proper hate-crime proceedings, which blunts the sentencing uplift the hate-crime provisions are meant to provide.  Public hostility remains organised and documented. The first Podgorica Pride, scheduled for May 2011, was cancelled after two attacks on gay people in the capital. The first Pride eventually marched in October 2013: roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, with rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 records continued anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric during 2023, alongside more than 222 reported online hate-speech incidents.  Trans-specific violence is documented. In 2023 a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on television was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks, with police response monitored. A visitor who is visibly gender non-conforming can expect verbal hostility and a realistic risk of physical confrontation at Pride or in visible public settings, even though the state deploys heavy police protection at such events.  The partnership law grants near marriage-equivalent rights through a registrar ceremony and explicitly excludes parenting, foster care and adoption. Hospital visitation and shared-benefit rights were absent before its adoption, which is why advocacy groups described LGBT people as living as second-class citizens in 2019; a 2018 study found 51% of LGBT Montenegrins were closeted.
